design_detail: Within-person pharmacokinetic study in 6 healthy men, each studied after a smoked condition (S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride vaporized from a heated glass device in the laboratory, about 30 mg placed in it, of which a mean of 21.8 mg was taken up) and after an intravenous condition (15.4–15.5 mg of the same salt over 1 minute). Methamphetamine and amphetamine were measured in plasma (to 48 h), urine (to 72 h) and saliva (to 24 h) by gas chromatography; pharmacokinetics were analysed by model-independent methods, with a compartmental model fitted to the urinary data and, post hoc, a two-input model to the plasma data. Subjective 'high' (0–100) and a full cardiovascular panel were recorded. No placebo condition; the order of the two conditions is not stated.
can_establish: Bioavailability, half-life, clearance, volume of distribution, urinary and renal handling of smoked and intravenous methamphetamine in 6 men, with each man as his own control, and the time course of subjective and cardiovascular effects relative to plasma concentrations in the same sessions.
cannot_establish: Anything about women, about people who use methamphetamine heavily or repeatedly, or about doses outside the narrow range studied; and no placebo-controlled statement about the effects themselves, since there was no placebo condition and the subjective scale was anchored to each man's own previous experience of amphetamines.

sample.recruitment: Six healthy paid male volunteers familiar with the use of amphetamines; the recruitment route is not described (p. 717).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Good health shown by medical and psychiatric history, physical examination, haematocrit, liver enzymes and body weight in relation to height and age; a normal diet; no tobacco use; a contract to avoid prescription, over-the-counter and recreational drugs during participation (p. 717).
sample.demographics: Mean age 26.7 years (SE 1.7), weight 83.8 kg (SE 5.1), height 176.4 cm (SE 1.5); all men. Nothing is reported about how much methamphetamine the participants usually used, how often or by which route (p. 717).
sample.attrition: None reported; all 6 appear in both conditions.
sample.selection_effects: Six healthy young men, non-smokers of tobacco, familiar with amphetamines but with their own use unquantified; this is a tolerance- and comorbidity-free sample, so the clearance and half-life estimates may not transfer to people who use methamphetamine heavily, and the subjective ratings are anchored to each man's own earlier experience.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered in the laboratory and measured directly: methamphetamine and amphetamine in plasma, urine and saliva by gas chromatography with a nitrogen-selective detector, with reported coefficients of variation of about 2–9% over the working range; the amount left in the device was recovered by rinsing and quantified by HPLC, so the absorbed dose was measured rather than assumed (pp. 717–718).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single smoked condition with about 30 mg of S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride placed in the device, of which participants took up a mean of 21.8 mg (SE 0.33; 17.5 mg as base), leaving 26.9% (SE 1.0) behind; and a single intravenous condition of 15.4–15.5 mg of the same salt (12.42 mg base) given over 1 minute. Each man received both (pp. 717–718).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were non-smokers of tobacco and contracted to avoid prescription, over-the-counter and recreational drugs during the study; no urine screening is described and no other drug use is quantified (p. 717).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported as a measured interval: participants agreed to avoid other drugs while taking part, and the interval between the two conditions is not stated.

comparison.controls: Each participant's intravenous condition is the reference for the smoked condition; there is no placebo and no non-using comparison group.
comparison.matching: Within-person; the order of conditions and the washout between them are not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic outcomes. For the subjective and cardiovascular measures there is no drug-free session, so only within-session pre-dose values serve as baseline.

outcomes.instruments: Gas chromatography with a nitrogen-selective detector for methamphetamine and amphetamine in plasma, urine and saliva; HPLC for the residue recovered from the device; model-independent pharmacokinetics (terminal rate constant, AUC, AUMC and derived parameters) with RS/1 and SAS, and ADAPT II for the urinary excretion model; a 0–100 'high' rating anchored at 100 to the highest the participant had ever experienced after taking amphetamines; heart rate and blood pressure by automated monitor, with stroke volume, cardiac output, systolic time intervals and myocardial contractility from impedance cardiography (pp. 717–718).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assays are validated in-house with stated precision; the subjective scale is self-anchored to the individual's own previous experience, so ratings are not comparable across people.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Bioavailability' is the fraction of the dose taken up from the device that reached plasma, computed from the AUC ratio against the same person's intravenous dose; 'acute tolerance' is inferred from effects subsiding while plasma concentrations were still high, not from any formal model.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About twelve statistical comparisons are reported (plasma versus urinary elimination rates by route, renal clearance and elimination rate constants between routes, two regressions of renal clearance on urine pH and flow, regressions of the fraction excreted and of the elimination rate constant on the absorbed dose, the amphetamine AUC comparison between routes, the methamphetamine-to-amphetamine urinary ratio between routes, and model comparisons), each at conventional thresholds.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None reported; the study was open and participants knew which condition they were receiving.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard errors (n=6), no confidence intervals. Bioavailability of the smoked condition 0.903 (SE 0.104) against the dose taken up from the device. Half-life: geometric mean 11.1 h smoked and 12.2 h intravenous; arithmetic mean 11.8 h (SE 1.35) and 13.1 h (SE 1.54), range across participants 8.3–18.2 h. AUC to infinity 1013 (SE 141) and 787 (SE 29.7) ng·mL⁻¹·h; mean residence time 16.7 (SE 1.46) and 17.4 (SE 2.15) h; total clearance (intravenous) 15.9 L/h (SE 0.73), or 0.192 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (SE 0.0097); volume of distribution in the elimination phase 3.24 (SE 0.36) and 3.73 (SE 0.59) L/kg, steady state 3.18 and 3.42 L/kg (Table 1, p. 719). Urine: 36.8% (SE 4.3) of the smoked and 45.0% (SE 9.5) of the intravenous dose excreted as methamphetamine over 72 h; renal clearance 6.68 (SE 0.80) and 6.95 (SE 1.25) L/h; metabolic clearance 57.9% and 55.0% of total clearance (Table 2, p. 719). Renal clearance depended on urine pH and flow: log clearance = −0.51 pH + 0.42 log flow + 4.58, r² 0.688, pH P = 0.0001, flow P = 0.013. The fraction of the absorbed dose excreted in urine fell as the absorbed dose rose (r² 0.901, P<0.005), and the elimination rate constant fell with increasing absorbed dose (r² 0.7042, P = 0.037) (pp. 720, 722).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person comparisons and simple regressions. Urine pH was deliberately not controlled, so that the kinetics would be measured under ordinary conditions (p. 720).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the study predates registry practice for pharmacokinetic work.
analysis.selective_reporting: The subjective and cardiovascular data for the smoked condition are largely referred back to the authors' earlier report on the same volunteers rather than given in full here; individual values are not shown for any parameter.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 6 participants and standard errors reported in place of standard deviations, the spread looks about two and a half times smaller than it is (SD = SE × √6, editors' note); the half-life range of 8.3–18.2 h across six men shows the real variability.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 6 men, methamphetamine taken up from a heated device reached the circulation almost completely (90% of the amount taken up), with a half-life of about 11 hours by that route and about 12 hours intravenously, a volume of distribution of 3.2–3.7 L/kg and clearance of about 0.19 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹; about 37–45% of the dose appeared unchanged in urine, with renal clearance strongly dependent on urine pH; amphetamine accounted for about 14–17% of the methamphetamine AUC. Subjective and cardiovascular effects peaked within about 12–18 minutes and had largely subsided while plasma concentrations were still high.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion that the effects subsiding before the plasma fall suggests acute tolerance goes beyond what was tested: no tolerance model was fitted, there was no placebo condition, and in 6 men with no repeated-dose arm the dissociation is a description of two time courses rather than a demonstrated tolerance mechanism. The abstract's bioavailability of 90.3% is relative to the amount taken up from the device, not to the amount placed in it, which is said only in the Results and Discussion; and the oral bioavailability of 67.2% is a calculation combining this study with an earlier one in different people. The pharmacokinetic conclusions themselves are stated carefully and match the tables, apart from the mean residence times (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: Clinical effects after methamphetamine vapour inhalation in the same volunteers (Perez-Reyes et al., 1991), from which the subjective and cardiovascular data here are partly drawn; the two reports are not independent
Oral methamphetamine pharmacokinetics and repeated daily dosing from the same group (Cook et al., 1992), the source of the oral comparison used here

Independent laboratory, 8 men: smoked bioavailability 37% of the dose placed in the device and about 67% of the amount estimated to have left it, with a half-life of 10.7 h — the half-life replicates, the bioavailability denominator differs
Oral sustained-release dosing in 8 volunteers: half-life 9.3–11.1 h, consistent with this study

replication.where_it_stands: The half-life (about 11–12 hours), volume of distribution (3–4 L/kg) and the dependence of renal clearance on urine pH have been reproduced by independent groups. The 90% figure for the smoked route is the highest in the literature and is defined against the amount taken up from the device; Harris et al. (2003) obtained 37% against the amount placed in the device and about 67% against the amount estimated delivered, so the figures are not interchangeable.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse contract 271-87-8126 (p. 717).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Research Triangle Institute and the University of North Carolina; one author's address at publication is given as Burroughs Wellcome Company (p. 717). Recorded as a flag, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover with a standardized delivery device reporting bioavailability against both the amount placed in it and the amount taken up, dense early sampling, urine pH measured and reported throughout, both sexes, and a repeated-dose arm with formal modelling of acute tolerance (effect against concentration with a hysteresis or tolerance term).

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two conditions)
domains.note: No randomization, allocation concealment, order or washout is described for the two conditions; the design is a within-person comparison of two open sessions.
Open administration with no placebo; the absorbed smoked dose (17.5 mg base) was larger than the intravenous dose (12.42 mg base), so the two conditions differ in dose as well as route.
All 6 participants contributed both conditions and all tabulated parameters; the two-input model was fitted to 4 of the 6 plasma profiles, which the authors state.

Assays, recovery from the device and cardiovascular measures are objective (low); the 'high' rating is a self-report in an unblinded session, anchored to each participant's own previous experience, so it cannot be compared across people (some concerns).

No protocol; the two-input model was fitted after the fact to explain the plasma plateau; subjective and cardiovascular results are partly deferred to an earlier paper on the same volunteers; standard errors are reported in place of standard deviations throughout.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the pharmacokinetic parameters the within-person design with a measured absorbed dose and a validated assay is appropriate, and the half-life, clearance and volume of distribution are the most reliable parts of the paper. The overall judgment is set by the unblinded, unrandomized, placebo-free design with unequal doses between conditions, which matters for the subjective and cardiovascular time courses and for the acute-tolerance inference. The source can be cited for the pharmacokinetic parameters of smoked and intravenous methamphetamine in 6 men, for the pH dependence of renal clearance, and for the observation that effects had subsided while plasma concentrations were still high; it cannot be cited as a demonstration of tolerance, nor for a bioavailability figure quoted without its denominator.

key_findings.finding: Bioavailability of the smoked condition was 90.3% (SE 10.4) of the dose taken up from the device; participants left a mean of 26.9% (SE 1.0) of the material behind, so the mean absorbed dose was 21.8 mg (SE 0.33) of the hydrochloride salt, or 17.5 mg (SE 0.26) as base.
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking Efficiency and Dose (p. 718, continuing on p. 719); Table 1, rows Dose, Dose (base) and f (p. 719)
key_findings.note: The denominator is the amount taken up, not the amount placed in the device; the paper states this in the Results and Discussion but not in the abstract.

key_findings.finding: Geometric mean plasma half-life was 11.1 h after the smoked condition and 12.2 h after the intravenous condition, with individual values ranging from 8.3 to 18.2 h; the arithmetic means in Table 1 are 11.8 h (SE 1.35) and 13.1 h (SE 1.54).
key_findings.locator: Results › Concentrations in Body Fluids and Pharmacokinetic Analysis (p. 718, last paragraph, continuing on p. 719); Table 1, Half-life row and footnotes b and c (p. 719)

key_findings.finding: Total clearance after the intravenous dose was 15.9 L/h (SE 0.73), or 0.192 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (SE 0.0097); the volume of distribution in the elimination phase was 3.24 L/kg (SE 0.36) after the smoked and 3.73 L/kg (SE 0.59) after the intravenous condition, with steady-state values of 3.18 and 3.42 L/kg.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Total clearance, Vd and Vss

key_findings.finding: Over 72 hours, 36.8% (SE 4.3) of the smoked and 45.0% (SE 9.5) of the intravenous dose were excreted in urine as unchanged methamphetamine; renal clearance was equivalent by route (6.68 and 6.95 L/h) and metabolic clearance accounted for 57.9% and 55.0% of total clearance.
key_findings.note: The percentages are of the dose taken up from the device (editors' calculation: 6.46/17.5 and 5.57/12.42 mg of base), not of the amount placed in it; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Renal clearance of methamphetamine depended on urine chemistry: log clearance = −0.51 × pH + 0.42 × log(flow rate) + 4.58 (r² = 0.688), with P = 0.0001 for pH and P = 0.013 for flow; urine pH was deliberately not controlled.

The fraction of the absorbed dose excreted unchanged in urine fell as the absorbed dose rose (linear regression across the oral, smoked and intravenous data, r² = 0.901, P<0.005), and the mean elimination rate constant also fell with increasing absorbed dose (r² = 0.7042, P = 0.037), which the authors read as possible dose-dependent kinetics with a saturable renal process.
key_findings.note: The regressions pool data from this study with an earlier oral study in different participants, so the dose range comes partly from another sample.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine, the active metabolite, reached an AUC of 125 (SE 14) ng·mL⁻¹·h after the smoked and 105 (SE 20) after the intravenous condition, about 14–17% of the methamphetamine AUC on a molar basis, with no significant difference between routes after correction for dose (P>0.7); urinary amphetamine was about 18–20% of methamphetamine on a molar basis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs beginning 'Amphetamine was found in both plasma and urine' and 'Amphetamine was also excreted in the urine'

key_findings.finding: Subjective 'high' peaked at 38% (SE 9.8) of each participant's own maximum after the smoked and 41.5% (SE 20.1) after the intravenous condition, at about 18 min (SE 2.1) and 17.4 min (SE 1.1) from the start of dosing; the maximum heart-rate change came at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8).
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph of p. 719 continuing on p. 720 (left column); Figure 3 (p. 720)
key_findings.note: The smoked-condition values are referred to the authors' earlier report on the same volunteers (reference 4), so they are not an independent measurement.

key_findings.finding: Subjective and cardiovascular effects had largely subsided while plasma concentrations were still high, which the authors interpret as acute tolerance; cardiovascular measures returned to baseline within a short period after both routes.

Plasma concentrations after the smoked condition showed a plateau rather than a simple peak; a model with a fast and a slow input function fitted 4 of the 6 participants, with absorption rate constants of 36.9 h⁻¹ (SE 7.5) and 0.693 h⁻¹ (SE 0.102), corresponding to absorption half-lives of 1.1 and 60 minutes, as the paper itself states (p. 722).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs beginning 'We had noted previously the difficulty of fitting' (p. 722) and continuing on p. 723; Figure 7 (p. 722)
key_findings.note: The slower input is attributed by the authors to material swallowed or retained and slowly released; the model was fitted after the plateau was observed.

key_findings.finding: The mean ratio of saliva to plasma concentration after the intravenous dose was 6.0, with coefficients of variation across time points averaging 50.8%; from 4 to 24 hours after the smoked condition the ratio averaged 5.1, after much higher early saliva values.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'For highly basic drugs such as methamphetamine'

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives mean residence times of 11.5 h (SE 0.5) and 11.3 h (SE 1.74) for the two routes, while Table 1 gives 16.7 h (SE 1.46) and 17.4 h (SE 2.15). The table's values are the ones consistent with the rest of the table: AUMC divided by AUC gives 16.9 h (smoked) and 17.2 h (intravenous) (editors' calculation from Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's mean residence times are wrong by about 5 hours and should not be quoted; the table values should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports geometric mean half-lives (11.1 and 12.2 h) while Table 1's main column reports arithmetic means (11.8 and 13.1 h), with the geometric means relegated to footnotes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different summary statistics circulate for the same parameter; a citation should say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states a smoked bioavailability of 90.3% without saying that the denominator is the amount taken up from the device rather than the amount placed in it; the qualification appears only in the Results and Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is routinely quoted as 'the bioavailability of smoked methamphetamine' and then compared with figures computed on a different denominator (Harris et al., 2003: 37% of the dose placed in the device).

reporting_issues.issue: The oral bioavailability of 67.2% (SE 3.1) given in the abstract is not a measurement in this study: it is calculated by combining these data with an earlier oral study in different participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: It must be cited as a cross-study calculation, not as an oral bioavailability measured in these six men.

reporting_issues.issue: Variability is reported as standard errors with n=6 throughout the tables and text, including for parameters with wide individual ranges (half-life 8.3–18.2 h).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers who take the reported dispersion as standard deviations will understate the between-person variability by a factor of about 2.4.

reporting_issues.issue: The subjective and cardiovascular data for the smoked condition are taken from the authors' earlier publication on the same volunteers, with the peak 'high' cited to that paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two reports are not independent observations and must not be counted as separate studies of the acute effects.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the percent of the dose recovered in urine as 36.8% (smoked) and 45.0% (intravenous), which match the urinary amount divided by the base dose in Table 1 (6.46 of 17.5 mg smoked, 5.57 of 12.42 mg intravenous; editors' calculation 36.9% and 44.8%); the denominator is therefore the dose taken up from the device, not the roughly 30 mg placed in it, whereas the abstract calls the quantity a percentage of the nominal dose without defining the term.
reporting_issues.consequence: The urinary fractions carry the same denominator problem as the bioavailability: read against the amount placed in the device, the fraction excreted would be lower, so the denominator must be quoted with the figure.

verification.checked_by: AI readers 10 and 11 (card check against the PDF) and the AI adjudicator

disagreements.first_pass: corresponding to absorption half-lives of about 1.1 minutes and 60 minutes (editors' calculation, 0.693 divided by each rate constant)
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (corrected): the rate constants are right (36.9, SE 7.5, and 0.693, SE 0.102 per hour) and the model fitted 4 of 6 profiles, but the absorption half-lives of about 1.1 and 60 minutes are printed by the paper itself (p. 722, immediately after the rate constants), so they are not an editors' calculation.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered p. 722: the paper states that the two rate constants are equivalent to absorption half-lives of 1.1 and 60 min. The attribution is corrected; the values are unchanged (0.693 divided by 36.9 per hour is 1.1 minutes, and by 0.693 per hour is 60 minutes).

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (missed): the denominator ambiguity extends beyond bioavailability: Table 2's percent of dose in urine (36.8% smoked, 45.0% intravenous) is computed against the administered base dose, that is the 17.5 mg taken up from the device, while the abstract calls it the nominal dose (6.46/17.5 = 36.9%, 5.57/12.42 = 44.8%).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered pp. 717 and 719 (Table 1 base doses 17.5 and 12.42 mg; Table 2 amounts 6.46 and 5.57 mg; abstract: 37-45% of the nominal dose). Added as a reporting issue. The reader's figure of a third is not carried over because it depends on assumptions about the amount placed in the device.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (missed, same item): the percent of dose in urine is computed against the administered base dose.
disagreements.resolution: Short note added to key finding 3 so that the denominator travels with the figures.
